a11y.what-is-a11y.explain:
- Accessibility, often abbreviated as **a11y** (11 letters between 'a' and 'y'), is the practice of designing and developing websites, applications, and digital tools so that people with permanent, temporary, or situational disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate, and interact with them effectively.

- It matters immensely because the internet is a public utility. Excluding users due to poor design is both unethical and often illegal under international laws (like the ADA or Section 508). For B.Tech CSE students building modern AI interfaces, accessible design ensures your applications reach the widest possible audience.

- Think of accessibility like building a physical public building: installing wheelchair ramps and automatic doors doesn't just help wheelchair users; it also helps people pushing strollers, delivery workers carrying heavy boxes, and cyclists.
how: Audit existing UI components for basic contrast and keyboard accessibility.
Implement semantic HTML tags (`<nav>`, `<main>`, `<button>`) instead of generic `<div>` elements.
Add descriptive `alt` text to all informative images.
Ensure full functionality using only a keyboard (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Escape).
Test your code using automated accessibility linters (like axe-core) and screen readers.
keyPoints: A11y stands for Accessibility (11 letters between a and y).
It includes visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive impairments.
Semantic HTML is the first and most critical line of defense for a11y.
Automated tools catch only about 30-50% of accessibility issues; manual testing is required.
Good accessibility improves SEO and general user experience (UX) for everyone.
mistakes: Mistake: Using `<div>` or `<span>` with click handlers instead of `<button>`. Fix: Always use native interactive elements to get built-in keyboard and screen reader support.
Mistake: Relying entirely on automated accessibility extensions. Fix: Always perform manual keyboard navigation tests.
Mistake: Assuming accessibility is only for the visually impaired. Fix: Design for motor, cognitive, and hearing needs as well.

a11y.disability-types.explain:
- Disabilities in digital accessibility are generally categorized into four primary pillars: **Visual** (blindness, low vision, color blindness), **Auditory** (deafness, hard of hearing), **Motor/Physical** (tremors, paralysis, missing limbs, inability to use a mouse), and **Cognitive** (ADHD, dyslexia, memory loss, learning difficulties).

- Furthermore, the Microsoft Inclusive Design model teaches us that disabilities are not just **permanent** conditions; they can also be **temporary** (e.g., a broken arm or eye surgery) or **situational** (e.g., trying to read a phone in bright sunlight or holding a baby while navigating with one hand).

- Recognizing these types matters because when you design for temporary or situational limitations, you drastically improve the user experience for everyone under various everyday environmental constraints.
how: Identify potential user limitations for the target application context.
Design flexible input methods (support touch, keyboard, voice, and mouse).
Ensure sufficient color contrast ratios to support color-blind and low-vision users.
Provide captions and transcripts for all audio and video content.
Write clear, plain-language text and maintain predictable page layouts for cognitive support.
keyPoints: Four main disability pillars: Visual, Auditory, Motor, and Cognitive.
Disabilities can be Permanent, Temporary, or Situational.
One-handed smartphone usage is a common situational motor limitation.
Bright glare causing temporary blindness is a situational visual limitation.
Inclusive design multiplies your audience reach across diverse real-world conditions.
mistakes: Mistake: Assuming all users can use a mouse. Fix: Ensure every interactive feature is fully operable via keyboard navigation.
Mistake: Conveying information solely through color (e.g., red text for error). Fix: Combine color with icons or text labels.
Mistake: Using complex, jargon-heavy error messages. Fix: Write clear, actionable instructions for cognitive ease.

a11y.wcag.explain:
- **WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines)** is the internationally recognized benchmark for web accessibility, developed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). Version 2.2 introduces updated criteria focusing heavily on mobile accessibility, cognitive accessibility, and low-vision users.

- WCAG is structured around four foundational principles, known by the acronym **POUR**: **Perceivable** (information must be presentable in ways users can perceive), **Operable** (interface components must be navigable), **Understandable** (information and UI operation must be clear), and **Robust** (content must be interpretable by a wide variety of assistive technologies).

- Compliance is measured across three distinct conformance levels: **A** (minimum accessibility), **AA** (the gold standard target for most commercial and educational websites and legal compliance), and **AAA** (highest, most stringent level of accessibility).
how: Review your website against the four POUR principles.
Target WCAG 2.2 Level AA conformance as your baseline requirement.
Verify color contrast: minimum 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.
Ensure keyboard focus indicators are clearly visible on all interactive items.
Test dynamic content updates with ARIA live regions for screen readers.
keyPoints: POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
Levels of conformance: A (lowest), AA (standard target), AAA (highest).
WCAG 2.2 adds new success criteria for focus appearance, dragging movements, and target sizes.
Normal text contrast ratio must be at least 4.5:1 for Level AA.
Every interactive element must not create keyboard traps.
mistakes: Mistake: Removing default CSS outline without providing a custom focus indicator. Fix: Always style `:focus` states clearly.
Mistake: Using low-contrast gray text on a white background. Fix: Check contrast ratios using automated developer tools.
Mistake: Setting WCAG Level AAA as a mandatory requirement for all projects when AA is the standard legal/commercial target. Fix: Aim for AA robustly first.

The **POUR Principles** are the four foundational pillars of web accessibility defined by the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). They stand for **Perceivable**, **Operable**, **Understandable**, and **Robust**.

Think of POUR like building a public library: **Perceivable** means books have large print or audio versions so everyone can sense them; **Operable** means the doors and shelves can be used by someone in a wheelchair; **Understandable** means the language and signs are clear; and **Robust** means the building can accommodate future modifications and works with various assistive devices.

Operable ensures interface components and navigation are workable.
Understandable ensures operation and information are clear.
Robust ensures content is interpreted reliably by various technologies.

a11y.a11y-laws.explain:
Accessibility laws are legal frameworks that mandate digital inclusion, ensuring that websites, software, and public infrastructure are accessible to individuals with disabilities.

These laws matter because without legal mandates, digital exclusion persists, leaving millions unable to access education, employment, and public services. Compliance is both a legal requirement and a social obligation for organizations.

Think of accessibility laws like building codes for physical structures: just as builders must include ramps and elevators by law, digital creators must include screen reader support and keyboard navigation.
how: Identify the jurisdiction and applicable laws (e.g., ADA in the US, RPwD Act in India).
Adopt recognized technical standards like WCAG as a benchmark for compliance.
Conduct regular accessibility audits and user testing with assistive technology users.
Maintain an accessibility statement and a feedback mechanism for users to report barriers.
keyPoints: ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act): Prohibits discrimination based on disability in public accommodations, including digital spaces in the US.
European Accessibility Act (EAA): Mandates digital accessibility across EU member states for key products and services.
RPwD Act (Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, India, 2016): Statutory framework for accessibility in India.
GIGW (Guidelines for Indian Government Websites): Standard for Indian government portals requiring WCAG compliance.
Failure to comply can lead to lawsuits, heavy fines, and reputational damage.
mistakes: Mistake: Assuming accessibility laws only apply to government websites. Fix: Commercial, educational, and e-commerce platforms are frequently targeted by lawsuits.
Mistake: Treating compliance as a one-time fix. Fix: Treat accessibility as an ongoing process integrated into the development lifecycle.
Mistake: Ignoring regional standards when deploying global apps. Fix: Comply with local laws such as GIGW in India or EAA in Europe.

a11y.assistive-tech.explain:
**Assistive Technologies (AT)** are hardware and software tools designed to help people with disabilities interact with digital systems.

These technologies matter because they bridge the gap between inaccessible software and the user, translating visual interfaces into speech, braille, or alternative physical controls.

Think of assistive technology like prescription glasses: just as glasses help a person with poor eyesight read a printed page, a screen reader helps a blind person navigate a software application.

a11y.landmarks.explain:
Landmarks are semantic HTML5 elements (`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`) that divide a web page into major functional sections. They matter because screen reader users rely on them to jump directly to content areas without listening to every word on the page, much like using an index or a table of contents in a textbook.

Think of a webpage like a large departmental store. Landmarks are the overhead signboards ("Grocery", "Electronics", "Billing") that instantly tell a customer where to go instead of wandering through every single aisle.

a11y.headings-a11y.explain:
Heading structure refers to the logical hierarchy of heading tags (`<h1>` to `<h6>`) on a web page. A proper heading outline provides an immediate structural map for users scanning visually or using screen readers.

Think of a heading structure like the chapters, sections, and sub-sections in a computer science textbook. You wouldn't jump straight from Chapter 1 to Chapter 5 without subheadings, and you wouldn't make a minor paragraph heading larger than the chapter title.
how: Use exactly one <h1> per page for the main page title.

Nest <h2> tags with <h3> tags for sub-sections, maintaining strict numerical hierarchy.
Never skip heading levels (e.g., jumping from <h2> to <h4>) as it breaks the document outline.
Use headings for document structure, not for visual styling or font sizing.
keyPoints: Screen readers allow users to jump from heading to heading to skim content.
Search engines (SEO) also rely heavily on correct heading hierarchy.
Skipping heading levels creates confusion and gives a false sense of missing content.
CSS should be used for styling and sizing, not the heading tag number.
Every view should ideally start with an <h1>.

Skipping levels (e.g., <h2> followed immediately by <h4>) + Fix: Ensure sequential incrementing like <h2> to <h3>.

a11y.accessible-names.explain:
An accessible name is the programmatic name computed by browsers and assistive technologies (like screen readers) for any interactive element or image on a webpage. When a screen reader user navigates to a button, link, or form input, it needs to announce a clear, concise name so the user knows what the control does.

Accessible names matter because standard visual labels (like text placed next to an input using CSS) are not automatically parsed by screen readers unless properly associated. Without an explicit accessible name, screen readers might just announce "button" or "input text", leaving visually impaired users completely guessing its purpose.

Think of an accessible name like a name tag worn by a customer service representative at a store. Even if they are standing behind a counter with various tools, their name tag tells you exactly who they are and how to address them without any ambiguity.
how: Use native semantic elements like `<label>` paired with the `for` attribute and an input's `id` attribute.
Use `aria-label` directly on an element when there is no visible text label available in the DOM.
Use `aria-labelledby` to point to the `id` of another element on the page that acts as the label text.
Leverage native inner text for elements like `` or `Home` which automatically compute as their accessible name.
keyPoints: Accessible names are computed by the browser using the Accessible Name and Description Computation (AccName) specification.
`aria-label` takes precedence over inner text for screen reader announcements.
`aria-labelledby` takes precedence over `aria-label` if both are present.
Form inputs must always have an associated accessible name to meet WCAG success criteria.

Mistake: Duplicating aria-label and visible text with conflicting information. Fix: Keep visible text and aria-label consistent or let native text do the work.

a11y.aria.explain:
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes defined by the W3C that you can add to HTML elements. It bridges the gap by telling assistive technologies about custom widgets, live updates, and structural relationships that standard HTML cannot express out of the box.

ARIA matters because modern web apps are built using generic tags like `<div>` and `<span>` styled to look like tabs, sliders, accordions, or dialogs. To a screen reader, a `<div>` with a click handler is just invisible noise. ARIA transforms these custom components into recognized UI controls with roles, states, and properties.

Live regions (`aria-live`) are a powerful accessibility feature in semantic HTML that allow developers to inform screen readers about dynamic changes on a webpage without requiring the user to move focus. When content updates inside a container marked with `aria-live`, assistive technologies automatically read the new text.

This matters immensely for modern Single Page Applications (SPAs) where components like live chat messages, stock ticker updates, or form submission spinners change asynchronously. Without `aria-live`, visually impaired users would remain completely unaware that background data had updated.

Think of a live region like a stadium announcer who speaks over the PA system whenever a goal is scored or a substitution happens, drawing the crowd's attention immediately without the spectators having to turn their heads to look at the scoreboard.

Fix: Keep a static wrapper in the DOM and only update its inner text content via JavaScript.

ARIA states and properties (`aria-expanded`, `aria-pressed`, `aria-current`, `aria-hidden`) communicate the current condition, value, or interactive state of UI widgets to assistive technologies. Unlike HTML attributes that rarely change, ARIA states are dynamic and frequently modified via JavaScript as users interact with the webpage.

In modern web development, custom components like accordions, toggle buttons, dropdown menus, and navigation breadcrumbs are built using generic elements like `<div>` or `<button>`. Without ARIA states, screen reader users have no idea whether a dropdown menu is currently open or closed, or which tab is active.

Think of ARIA states like the indicator lights on a car dashboard: when you turn on the high beams, a blue light illuminates on the dashboard. Similarly, when a user expands an accordion menu, `aria-expanded="true"` lights up the screen reader's virtual dashboard so the user knows the content is now visible.

Use `aria-current="page"` (or `step`, `location`, `date`) on navigation links to identify the item representing the current view.

Accessible forms ensure that every user—regardless of whether they use a mouse, keyboard, or screen reader—can successfully understand, fill out, and submit form fields. This involves pairing every input with a explicit `<label>`, providing clear instructions, linking descriptive error messages using `aria-describedby`, and marking invalid fields with `aria-invalid`.

Forms are the primary conversion point of the web (login, registration, checkout). If a form is inaccessible, users with disabilities are entirely locked out of essential online services, e-commerce, and educational portals.

Think of an accessible form like a well-designed paper tax form where every input box has a clear, bold title printed directly next to it, and instructions explicitly state 'Enter 10-digit mobile number' right beneath the box so there is zero ambiguity.

`aria-describedby` can chain multiple IDs separated by spaces for combining helper text and error descriptions.

a11y.roving-tabindex.explain:
Roving tabindex is a technique used to manage keyboard focus within a group of related interactive widgets—such as toolbars, tab lists, menus, or grids—using the arrow keys instead of the `Tab` key.

Instead of having every item in the widget reachable via `Tab`, only **one** item in the group has `tabindex="0"` at any given time (meaning it is in the page tab order). All other items in the group have `tabindex="-1"`. As the user presses arrow keys, the active item's `tabindex` is updated to `0` and focus is shifted to it, while previous items are reset to `-1`.

Think of a TV remote control's directional pad: pressing the `Tab` key brings you onto the remote as a single tab stop, and once you are there, you use the Up/Down/Left/Right arrows to move between channels or volume buttons without having to tab past every single button on the remote.

a11y.color-contrast.explain:
Colour contrast refers to the luminance difference between text and its background. Under Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 AA standards, normal text requires a minimum contrast ratio of `4.5:1`, while large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold) and UI components require at least `3:1`. This ensures that visually impaired users or those viewing screens in bright sunlight can easily read the content.

Failing to meet these ratios makes applications inaccessible to millions, leading to poor user experiences and potential legal compliance violations.

Think of it like reading a highway billboard at dusk: if the text is dark blue on a black background, it is unreadable. You need high-contrast colours like black on yellow or white on dark blue.

The `prefers-reduced-motion` media query detects if the user has requested that the system minimize non-essential motion. This is crucial for users with vestibular disorders, who can experience dizziness, nausea, or headaches from parallax scrolling, zooming, or flashing animations.

It matters because users with motor impairments, tremors, large fingers, or low vision struggle to click or tap tiny targets, leading to frustration and input errors.

Captions are time-synchronized text displayed on video; transcripts are static text documents containing all spoken and audio content.

a11y.plain-language.explain:
Plain language and readability involve writing content that users can understand the very first time they read or hear it. In digital accessibility, this is crucial for individuals with cognitive disabilities, dyslexia, or non-native speakers, helping them navigate applications without confusion.

Why it matters: Complex jargon, convoluted sentences, and inconsistent terminology increase cognitive load. When interfaces use clear, direct language and maintain a consistent UI copy, users make fewer errors and complete tasks faster.

Analogy: Think of a road sign. Instead of saying `Proceed cautiously along the optimal vehicular trajectory`, it simply says `Slow Down`. Plain language is the `Slow Down` sign of digital interfaces.
how: Write short, direct sentences focusing on a single idea.
Avoid unnecessary technical jargon or complex acronyms; define them if used.
Use active voice instead of passive voice to make instructions clear.
Structure text with clear headings, bullet points, and ample whitespace.
Ensure consistent naming conventions for interactive elements across the app.
keyPoints: Plain language helps users with cognitive and learning disabilities.
Target a lower secondary education reading level for general content.
Consistent terminology prevents user disorientation.
Bullet points and bold text improve scannability.
Always test content with real users from diverse backgrounds.
mistakes: Mistake: Using overly formal or legalistic language. Fix: Simplify sentences into everyday conversational terms.
Mistake: Mixing terminology (e.g., using 'Sign In', 'Log In', and 'Sign Up' interchangeably). Fix: Choose one term and stick to it site-wide.
Mistake: Writing massive paragraphs of unbroken text. Fix: Break text into chunks of 3-4 lines maximum.

a11y.dark-mode-a11y.explain:
Dark mode and high contrast support allow users to adjust interface brightness and colour palettes according to their environmental needs and visual conditions like photophobia or low vision.

Why it matters: Standard light themes can cause glare and eye strain in low-light environments. Conversely, poorly implemented dark modes with pure black (#000000) and pure white (#FFFFFF) can cause text halation and eye fatigue for astigmatism users. Proper contrast ensures legibility for colour-blind and low-vision users.

Analogy: Think of wearing sunglasses on a bright day versus turning on a desk lamp in a dark room. Both regulate light to protect your vision and keep text readable.
how: Respect the user's operating system preferences using the CSS `prefers-color-scheme` media query.
Use CSS custom properties (variables) to dynamically swap theme colour tokens.
Ensure text meets WCAG contrast ratios (at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text).
Avoid pure black backgrounds (#000000); use dark gray tones (#121212) to reduce smearing on OLED screens.
Test colour contrast using automated tools like axe or Chrome DevTools.
keyPoints: Respects OS-level theme settings automatically.
WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 contrast; AAA requires 7:1 for normal text.
Pure black and white can cause severe eye strain and halation.
Use CSS variables for scalable and maintainable theme switching.
Test for colour-blindness using simulation tools.
mistakes: Mistake: Hardcoding colours in components without supporting dark mode tokens. Fix: Use CSS variables that update based on theme classes or media queries.
Mistake: Using low-contrast gray text on a dark gray background. Fix: Verify contrast ratios using a WCAG checker.
Mistake: Relying solely on colour to convey critical status information. Fix: Add text labels or icons alongside colour cues.

Via the `prefers-color-scheme` media query.

a11y.screen-readers.explain:
Screen readers (such as NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, and TalkBack) are assistive technologies that translate digital content into synthesized speech or refreshable braille displays for blind and severely visually impaired users.

Why it matters: Developers often build visually stunning interfaces using unsemantic HTML (like `<div>` soup). Screen readers rely entirely on the underlying DOM and ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) tree to understand structure and interactive states. If markup is broken, the screen reader user is locked out.

Analogy: Think of a screen reader as an interpreter translating a foreign play into an audio description for an audience member who cannot see the stage.
how: Use native semantic HTML elements (`<button>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`) before reaching for ARIA.
Provide descriptive `alt` text for all informative images.
Manage keyboard focus visibility and logical tab order (`tabindex`).
Use ARIA landmarks (`role="region"`, `aria-label`) only when native HTML is insufficient.
Test your application manually using real screen readers like NVDA (Windows) or VoiceOver (macOS/iOS).
keyPoints: Screen readers read the accessibility tree, not the visual layout.
NVDA and JAWS are dominant on Windows; VoiceOver is built into Apple ecosystems.
Native HTML has built-in accessibility semantics; `div` elements do not.
ARIA attributes modify or enhance how elements are announced.
Keyboard accessibility and screen reader navigation go hand in hand.
mistakes: Mistake: Using `<div>` elements with click handlers instead of `<button>`. Fix: Use native buttons which have built-in screen reader announcements and focus states.
Mistake: Writing redundant alt text like `alt="image of logo"`. Fix: Write descriptive alt text like `alt="Company Logo"` or `alt=""` for decorative images.

Mistake: Hiding visible content from screen readers using `display: none` when it should be announced. Fix: Use CSS utility classes like `.sr-only` only when hiding visual elements that screen readers need.

a11y.axe.explain:
Axe DevTools is an accessibility testing engine built into browser developer tools and automated test suites. It detects WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) violations directly in your DOM.

It matters because automated testing catches up to 50% of known accessibility bugs instantly during development, saving hours of manual remediation.

Think of Axe DevTools as a smoke detector for your website's accessibility: it won't tell you if the house is beautifully decorated, but it will instantly scream if there is a fire hazard like a missing alt tag or a contrast failure.
how: Install the Axe DevTools browser extension in Chrome, Firefox, or Edge.
Open your target web page and launch Developer Tools (F12).
Navigate to the 'Axe DevTools' or 'Accessibility' tab.
Click 'Scan ALL of my page' to execute the automated ruleset.
Review identified violations, inspect highlighted DOM nodes, and follow the provided remediation guidance.
keyPoints: Axe is open-source and built on the axe-core rules engine.
Zero false positives is a core design goal of the axe-core engine.
Can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines via Playwright, Cypress, or Jest (axe-webdriverjs).
Scans live DOM trees, checking rendered states dynamically.
Categorizes issues by impact level: Minor, Moderate, Serious, Critical.
mistakes: Mistake: Relying solely on Axe for 100% compliance. Fix: Remember automated tools only catch about 30-50% of accessibility errors; manual testing is still mandatory.
Mistake: Ignoring minor impact issues. Fix: Address all warnings early before they compound into major barriers.
Mistake: Scanning static markup without interacting with the page. Fix: Trigger dynamic states (modals, dropdowns) before running the scan.

theory: What is axe-core?
It is the underlying open-source JavaScript accessibility testing engine used by Axe DevTools and various testing frameworks.
Why does Axe claim zero false positives?
Because its rules are rigorously tested against W3C and WCAG standards to ensure a rule only fires when a definite violation exists.
Can Axe test custom widget keyboard navigation?
Partially, but complex keyboard trap testing and screen reader announcements require manual verification.
How do you run Axe in a CI/CD pipeline?
By integrating libraries like @axe-core/playwright or cypress-axe into test automation scripts.
What impact levels does Axe report?
Critical, Serious, Moderate, and Minor.

a11y.lighthouse-a11y.explain:
Lighthouse is an open-source, automated tool by Google for improving the quality of web pages. Its Accessibility audit checks pages against a subset of WCAG rules and outputs an overall score from 0 to 100.

It matters because high Lighthouse scores correlate with better SEO, broader user reach, and adherence to modern web standards.

Think of a Lighthouse accessibility audit as an annual health checkup at the clinic: it gives you a quick numerical score and a checklist of lifestyle changes to improve your overall health.
how: Open Google Chrome and navigate to the webpage you want to audit.
Open Developer Tools (F12) and select the 'Lighthouse' tab.
Check the 'Accessibility' category box (you can uncheck others for speed).
Select your device mode (Mobile or Desktop).
Click 'Analyze page load' and wait for the report to generate.
keyPoints: Lighthouse accessibility score is calculated based on passed vs. failed audits weighted by importance.
Runs directly in Chrome DevTools or via Node.js CLI / PageSpeed Insights.
Provides clear links to documentation for fixing each flagged audit.
Tests server-rendered and initial client-rendered DOM states.
Can be automated in CI pipelines using Lighthouse CI (LHCI).
mistakes: Mistake: Optimizing only for desktop Lighthouse scores. Fix: Always audit mobile viewports since mobile accessibility issues are often more severe.
Mistake: Chasing a 100 score while ignoring real screen reader testing. Fix: Lighthouse is automated; real human assistive tech testing is still required.
Mistake: Running audits on localhost without simulated throttling or clean cache. Fix: Run audits in Incognito mode with extensions disabled for accurate results.

a11y.manual-testing.explain:
Manual accessibility testing involves human evaluation of web interfaces using assistive technologies such as screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS) and navigating strictly via keyboard (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape).

It matters because automated tools cannot evaluate user experience, logical tab order, clarity of alt-text context, or whether screen reader announcements actually make sense to a blind user.

Think of manual testing like test-driving a car yourself after the factory robots check the engine: automated tools check if the bolts are tight, but only a human driver can tell if the steering wheel feels natural and responsive.
how: Unplug or put away your mouse/trackpad.
Attempt to navigate the entire web page using only the `Tab` and arrow keys.
Verify that a visible focus indicator is present on every interactive element at all times.
Launch a screen reader (e.g., NVDA on Windows or VoiceOver on macOS).
Close your eyes or turn off your monitor, and listen to whether the page reads logically and completely.
keyPoints: Keyboard navigation test: Check for focus traps and logical tab order (left-to-right, top-to-bottom).
Screen reader test: Ensure landmark regions (`<main>`, `<nav>`, `<header>`) are announced correctly.
Color independence: Verify information is not conveyed by color alone (e.g., error fields marked with text or icons, not just red borders).
Zoom test: Zoom the page up to 200% without horizontal scrolling breaking layout or content overlapping.
Touch target size: Ensure mobile interactive targets are at least 48x48 CSS pixels.
mistakes: Mistake: Using `outline: none` in CSS without providing a custom replacement focus style. Fix: Always ensure a high-contrast `:focus` or `:focus-visible` ring.
Mistake: Assuming native HTML elements are always fully accessible when heavily styled. Fix: Test styled inputs and dropdowns with actual screen readers.
Mistake: Testing with a mouse while pretending to test accessibility. Fix: Physically disconnect the mouse to force strict keyboard usage.
